# Documentation Standard

**Last Updated:** 2026-05-11
**Purpose:** Defines the structure, conventions, and expectations for all documentation in the MDC platform. Covers development planning docs (roadmaps, phase files, sprints), operator guides, and the deferred-work convention.

**History:** This standard was originally `development/dev_docs_standard.md` and focused narrowly on development planning files. Relocated to `standards/documentation/documentation_standard.md` on 2026-04-16 and expanded to cover the full documentation hierarchy: development planning, operator guides, sprint tracking, and loose-ends management.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Repository Structure Overview

`mdc-master-planning/` is the single source of truth for all MDC platform standards and documentation.

```
mdc-master-planning/
├── standards/          # Platform-wide standards (this doc, architecture, development, etc.)
├── development/        # Implementation planning and tracking
│   ├── sprints.md      # Sprint execution plan (what's being built and when)
│   ├── common/         # Cross-cutting concerns (genesis, bootstrap, DAS, harbor, close_out/)
│   ├── infra/          # Layer 1: physical hosts
│   ├── vm/             # Layer 2: VM lifecycle
│   ├── container/      # Layer 3: container runtime, K3s, ArgoCD
│   ├── service/        # Platform services (monitoring, secrets, skyy-gate, etc.)
│   └── workload/       # Customer workloads (Synaptron, OpenClaw, etc.)
├── guide/              # Operator manual (user-facing)
└── business_planning/  # Business model, tokenomics, strategy
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Standards Corpus Organization (binding)

`standards/` is organized **by concern/technology** (`ansible/`, `temporal/`, `argocd/`, `networking/`, `secrets/`, …), **not** by the six-domain model. Most standards are cross-cutting and don't fit one domain — forcing the tree to mirror the runtime architecture would orphan them and create a second axis to maintain. (The six-domain model IS binding for the desired-state repo, chart library, Ansible collections, and Temporal modules — but those hold *artifacts*, not *standards*.)

### Vehicle-lifecycle grid — `platform_deployment/` (binding)

Where a domain folder collects the **lifecycle standards for the platform's compute vehicles**, name them on a two-axis grid: **`<vehicle>_<management|clustering>_standard.md`**, where `vehicle ∈ {host, vm, container}`.

| | `_management` (the individual entity) | `_clustering` (orchestrating many) |
|---|---|---|
| **host** | `host_management_standard.md` | `host_clustering_standard.md` *(reserved — Proxmox/corosync; written when host-orchestration is codified)* |
| **vm** | `vm_management_standard.md` | *(name reserved; no content today)* |
| **container** | *(individual workload = `kubernetes/` + `argocd/`)* | `container_clustering_standard.md` *(K3s clusters)* |

**The rules that keep this from rotting:**
1. **A file exists only when it carries binding content.** An empty cell is a *reserved name*, never a stub doc. This is what prevents a future graveyard of hollow `*_clustering` files.
2. **The unit of management differs per vehicle, and that is correct** — host's unit is the individual host (clustering is a separate cross-host fabric concern); container's unit IS the cluster (individual containers are `kubernetes/`+`argocd/`). The *same rule* applied honestly yields different-looking results because the vehicles genuinely differ. Forcing identical doc-shapes onto non-identical concerns is the anti-pattern.
3. **Mechanism/fabric SSOTs stay in their by-concern folder and are cross-referenced, never duplicated** (e.g. `container_clustering` → `kubernetes/` + `argocd/` for what-runs-*on* the cluster; `host_clustering` → `networking/` for the corosync VLAN).

`host_filesystem_standard.md` also lives in `platform_deployment/` (host `/opt/skyy-net/` ownership/ACLs) — host-adjacent, but not part of the vehicle grid.

## Component vs phase — what gets a folder (binding)

**Promoted out of § Development Planning Files deliberately, and it survives any exclusion of that section.** The decision below asks *what kind of thing this work is* — it is layout-independent and binds every repo. It previously sat nested inside a layout-specific section, and a consuming repo that legitimately excluded that section therefore lost the rule: **three separate runs read the exclusion correctly, concluded this did not bind, and fell back to a local convention.** Each run was right; each left a binding rule unapplied. A rule that binds everywhere must not depend on a section some consumers correctly exclude.

A recurring failure mode: work that is neither a roadmap nor a phase doc gets dropped in as a **standalone named design doc** (`some_design.md`, `*_notes.md`, `*_plan.md`). **There is no such category.** Every planning doc is exactly one of two things:

- **A new component** — a distinct domain of work (a service, a subsystem, a cross-domain program) — gets its **own folder** with the full structure.
- **A new phase of an EXISTING component** — work that falls under a component that already has a roadmap — is **just one more phase doc** in that component's folder plus a row in its roadmap. No new folder, no second roadmap.

**Decide with one question: does this work stand up a new domain, or extend an existing one?** New domain → component. Extends an existing domain → a phase under it. If you find yourself writing a `*_design.md` that is neither, you skipped this decision — go back and pick.

**The DECISION is binding everywhere; the ARTIFACT SHAPES are not.** `roadmap.md` + `phase{N}_{name}.md` is the shape § Development Planning Files prescribes for repos using that layout. A repo with a different layout applies the same decision and supplies its own artifacts — it does not get to skip the decision because the filenames differ.

**A component with no plan yet is UNPLANNED, not non-conformant (binding).** This section governs work that is *being planned*; it does not convert every un-started component into a violation. A folder that exists as a placeholder, or a component named in a roadmap but not yet elaborated, is simply unplanned — a state, not a defect. **Without this, a standard mandating structure reads as an indictment of everything not yet begun**, which trains readers to ignore conformance reports rather than act on them. Non-conformance begins when planning starts and takes the wrong shape.

*(Exempt — NOT planning docs, so this rule does not govern them: `research/` notes, workflow-generated `dependencies.md`/`requirements.md`/`review-resolutions.md`, archived `old/` + `old_files_for_reference/` material, and `CLAUDE.md`.)*

## Development Planning Files

Every development domain (infra, vm, container, service, workload, etc.) uses these file types. **The component-vs-phase decision is made above and is not repeated here** — this section supplies the artifact shapes for repos using this layout.

### 1. Roadmap (`roadmap.md`)

The overview for a domain or feature area. Written for quick understanding, not implementation.

**Structure:**
- One paragraph per phase describing what it achieves (not how)
- 3-5 checkboxes per phase (completion criteria, not implementation steps)
- Links to each phase file
- Dependencies on other domains listed explicitly
- Current status clearly marked at the top

**Rules:**
- Keep concise — if a phase description exceeds one paragraph, the scope is too broad
- Checkboxes are marked only when the phase is genuinely complete
- **Deferred work does not live in roadmap docs or phase docs.** It is a file in [`tracked/issues/`](../../tracked/) — see [Tracked Items Standard](./tracked_items_standard.md). A roadmap or phase doc that carries an inline "Loose Ends" section is legacy; its items are triaged into issues, not maintained in place.
- This is the file a PM or new team member reads first

### 2. Phase Implementation (`phase{N}_{name}.md`)

The working document for a specific phase. Written for the developer doing the work.

**Structure:**
- **Requirements for completion** clearly stated at the top (what "done" means)
- **Dependencies** on other phases or domains
- Ordered checklist of implementation steps with checkboxes
- Testing and verification steps included in the checklist (not separate)
- Notes, decisions, and gotchas captured inline as they arise

**Rules:**
- Can be long — this is the working doc, detail is expected
- Checkboxes are marked only when the step is actually complete and verified
- Each phase should stop at a logical point of functionality (something works end-to-end)
- If a phase grows beyond what's manageable, split it — don't let a single phase become a project
- **Prove manually before automating.** For new pipelines or integrations, the first phase should prove the mechanics work by hand. Automation phases follow once the manual process is proven and documented. This prevents building automation on top of untested assumptions
- **Live-runtime verification before engineer dispatch (binding — see below)** for any phase doc that orchestrates an external runtime (cloudflared, nginx, Vault, Tailscale, etc.)

### Live-Runtime Verification (binding)

**Binding.** Any phase doc that orchestrates an external runtime (a daemon, a service, a vendor API) MUST include explicit verification of the runtime model BEFORE the engineer dispatch fires. Documentation describes intent; running systems define reality. When the two diverge, the phase doc is wrong AND the engineer's implementation will be wrong.

**What to verify and document in the phase doc (as a "Runtime Assumptions" or "Live-Runtime Verification" section):**

- **Process startup mode** — `systemctl cat <unit>` output showing the actual `ExecStart` args (e.g., does cloudflared run with `--config <file>` or `--token`?)
- **File paths the daemon actually reads** — `lsof -p <pid>` or `strace` to confirm the daemon's open files match the config files the phase doc proposes to edit
- **Listening ports / sockets** — `ss -tlnp` to confirm the runtime exposes what the phase doc plans to consume
- **Versions and modes** — `<daemon> --version` + any mode-determining flags
- **Config file ownership of state** — for any file the workflow will mutate, prove the daemon reads it (e.g., temporarily change a known-effect field, restart, observe behavior change)

**When to do it:**

- BEFORE writing the implementation-step checklist — runtime verification informs the implementation, not the other way around
- The verification output (or pointers to it) goes IN THE PHASE DOC, not in a side scratch file
- For long-lived runtimes that change over time, re-verify each time the phase doc is touched substantively (e.g., a Phase 2 update should re-verify the assumptions from Phase 1's verification block)

**Why the binding:** the 2026-05-15 customer-browser PR #84 was built on a planning-doc claim that cloudflared on SkyyGate ran with `--config /etc/cloudflared/config.yml` (local-config mode). The actual daemon ran with `--token <UUID>` (tunnel-API mode); the repo's `cloudflared/config.yml` was dead code nothing read. Eight iterations of fix commits + a complete architecture rewrite (2026-05-26) followed. The planning doc cited a stale `deployment-guide.md` description; nobody (PM, engineer, peer-review agents) verified against the running daemon before committing. Adding live-runtime verification as a binding planning-stage gate closes this class — a 60-second `systemctl cat cloudflared` would have surfaced the mode mismatch immediately.

**Breaking it looks like:** a phase doc that asserts "the daemon reads file X" or "the daemon runs in mode Y" without an inline verification block or a citation to a verified source; a phase doc that cites another doc's description of runtime behavior without re-verifying it; a phase doc whose Implementation Steps interact with files / ports / config the verification block doesn't enumerate.

**Enforcement — `§Runtime Verification` section is REQUIRED in the phase doc itself (binding).** The discipline above is insufficient on its own — the rule's first violation was the very PR that introduced it (mdc-master-planning PR #54, customer-browser cloudflared re-architecture, merged `f83a1b2` — the rewritten phase doc still claimed "nginx already running for helloskyy.io website" without verification; live state showed no nginx installed; surfaced during the next engineer dispatch's pre-flight on 2026-05-27). The peer-review agents and PM3 both missed it because the verification was a discipline ("you should verify") rather than an artifact ("show your work in the doc"). The amendment closes that gap:

Every phase doc that orchestrates an external runtime MUST contain an explicit `§Runtime Verification` section showing:

1. **The verification commands run** — verbatim, copy-pasteable, reproducible
2. **The actual outputs observed** — verbatim from live state (with secrets redacted using `<REDACTED>` placeholders); not paraphrased, not summarized
3. **The date the verification was performed** — so reviewers can judge staleness
4. **The host(s) verified against** — so the verification scope is unambiguous

A phase doc that has a `§Runtime Verification` section with the items above present is treated as having satisfied the live-runtime verification rule. A phase doc without the section is treated as NOT having satisfied it, regardless of whether verification happened informally. This is an artifact requirement — the artifact MUST be in the doc.

**Re-verification on substantial revision:** when a phase doc is substantially revised (architectural change, scope expansion, target-runtime change), the `§Runtime Verification` section MUST be re-run and updated. A "Last verified: 2026-05-15" entry that wasn't refreshed during a 2026-05-27 rewrite is a violation.

**Companion: compensation correctness.** Phase docs whose workflow includes compensation activities (saga pattern) MUST cite [Stateful Patterns Standard §6.6](../development/temporal/stateful_patterns.md) — compensation activities verify effect before returning ok, and tests assert post-compensation state. Live-runtime verification and compensation correctness are the planning-stage and execution-stage halves of the same discipline.

### Phase Numbering and Roadmap Ordering (binding)

Phase docs serve two distinct purposes that must be kept separate: tracking work (identity) and conveying logical structure (ordering). Conflating them creates the renaming-and-cross-reference cost that recurs every time work is added to an existing roadmap. The following rules eliminate that cost.

**Three orderings, three concerns:**

| Layer | Mutable? | Conveys | Lives in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase number | NO | identity (like a ticket number) | **the filename ONLY** — see rule 4 |
| Roadmap position | YES | logical rollout order within the domain | `roadmap.md` ordering |
| Sprint position | YES | execution order across all domains | `sprints.md` |

**Guiding principle:** Live docs are the source of truth; git history is the archaeology layer. The roadmap describes the project NOW; commit history describes the path TO now. When deciding whether to retain a tombstone entry vs delete a relocated one, ask: *"does this entry serve a reader who lacks git access?"* If the breadcrumb is recoverable in under two minutes from `git log` or `git blame`, it does not need to live in the live doc. Pristine live docs set the pattern that future planning dispatches (human and agent) match against — drift in exemplars propagates to drift in new work.

**Rules:**

1. **Phase numbers are immutable creation-order identifiers.** A new phase takes the next sequential number not yet used in this roadmap (`max(existing) + 1`). Phase numbers never renumber. Gaps in the sequence are fine — they reflect canceled or relocated phases.

2. **Roadmap entries are listed in logical rollout order**, NOT phase-number order. The order describes how the work would happen within the domain if there were no cross-domain dependencies. New phases are inserted at their correct logical position; their phase number does not change to match that position. A roadmap may legitimately list Phase 10 between Phase 1 and Phase 2.

3. **Implementation order lives in `sprints.md`**, which interleaves phases from multiple roadmaps based on cross-domain dependencies and capacity. Sprint order may diverge from both phase-number order and roadmap-position order; that is expected.

4. **A phase is CITED BY NAME, never by number (binding, 2026-08-20).**

   **THE FORWARD RULE, AND IT BINDS FROM NOW: anything newly written names the phase.** *"ESO Deployment"*, never *"Phase 6"*. This half costs nothing, applies everywhere including inside phase docs, and is the half that matters most — **it stops the backlog growing while the backlog is being worked.** A new document that cites a phase by number is a defect regardless of what its component's conversion state is.

   **The number survives in the FILENAME and nowhere else.** `phase12_per_cluster_vault_scoping.md` keeps its digit permanently. **This is a hard external constraint, not a preference:** the `plan-feature` / `plan-verify` family discovers phase docs with `^phase(\d+)([a-z]?)_[a-z0-9_-]+\.md$`. Rename the file and the component reports **zero phase docs** — nothing gets sized, the plan inventory is empty, and `taken_phase_numbers()` returns nothing so the next new phase numbers from 1 and **collides with a live identity**. Treat it as a primary key: required by the machinery, never shown to the reader. Removing it for real is an upstream tooling change first.

   **Why naming at all, and it follows from rules 1 and 2 above.** The number conveys *creation order*; the roadmap lists in *build order*. A reader seeing `0 → 12 → 6 → 13 → 7` down a roadmap cannot tell correct from corrupt, and re-derives that doubt every time. Naming removes the question rather than explaining it, and costs nothing — **a phase's name is exactly as stable as its number.**

   ### Converting what already exists — scope is BOUNDED (binding)

   **Three surfaces convert. A fourth explicitly does not.**

   | Surface | Convert? | Why |
   |---|---|---|
   | `sprints.md` entries | **yes** | the cross-component browse surface |
   | `roadmap.md` — headings and prose | **yes** | the within-component browse surface |
   | Phase-doc **titles** (the `# ` line) | **yes** | what a tab, a grep hit and a search result show — a result should identify itself without its directory |
   | Phase-doc **internal prose** | **NO — deliberately** | see below |

   **Phase-doc internals are left alone on a measured cost argument, not an aesthetic one.** Corpus-wide the split is **1,469 references in roadmaps, 48 in `sprints.md`, and 3,417 inside phase docs** — so converting internals is **69% of the total work for the surface a reader is least often browsing**, because by the time you are reading a phase doc's body you are already working inside that phase.

   > **The accepted residual, stated rather than hidden:** a phase doc saying *"gated on Phase 8"* still makes a reader look up what Phase 8 is, and **that is exactly the case where a name would help**, because it points at a phase they are *not* in. This is a known cost, accepted deliberately to keep the migration finite. Revisit it if it actually bites; do not re-litigate it because it looks untidy.

   **Migration is opportunistic, never a sweep.** A component converts when someone is already working in it. **Under this narrowed scope a typical component is a roadmap plus one title — tens of references, not hundreds.** *(The secrets component: **99** under this rule, against **519** under the scope this section previously described.)*

   **Three components were converted before this narrowing** — Tailscale, firewall and github-automation — and their phase-doc internals are done too. **They are ahead of the requirement, not in violation of it.** Do not revert them.

   **A cross-reference is a NAME plus a LINK, and never a POSITION.** Write `[ESO Deployment](phase6_eso.md)` — never *"the next phase," "the previous phase,"* or *"the second phase in roadmap X."* **The anti-positional half predates this rule and survives it unchanged**; only its instruction to cite the *number* was superseded. Positions break silently when a roadmap is reordered, and rule 2 explicitly permits reordering.

   > *This paragraph replaces a second rule that was also numbered **4** and read "cross-references use phase numbers only" — the two sat nine lines apart and gave opposite instructions, so a component converting its references could cite either and be quoting a binding rule. **The collision was introduced by the 2026-08-20 edit that added this rule without retiring the one it superseded**, and both halves of that older rule are preserved above: the number instruction was genuinely replaced, the anti-positional instruction was not. Merged 2026-08-22, closing issue #157.*

   **Breaking it looks like:** a **newly written** reference to a phase by number, anywhere, including inside a phase doc; `Phase 7` surviving in a converted roadmap, sprint entry or phase-doc title; a phase doc renamed to drop its filename digit; a component whose roadmap is converted while its own title lines are not; or a **positional** reference of any kind, which is a defect under this rule in both its old and new form.

5. **Closed and deprecated phases keep their entry.** Use status markers (`[x]` for closed, `[~]` or `DEPRECATED` prefix for canceled/superseded). Do not delete entries to fill number gaps — gaps are correct; missing entries leave readers wondering what was removed. **Phase numbers of closed or deprecated phases are NOT reusable** — external references in code comments, commit messages, and sprint docs may still point at them, and reusing the number creates silent ambiguity.

   **Relocations differ from deprecations.** When a phase's planning is moved to a different roadmap or a different abstraction (loose-ends, sprint sub-item, peer roadmap) BEFORE implementation, that is a relocation, not a deprecation. The entry MAY be deleted from the original roadmap with all cross-references redirected to the new canonical home — git history preserves the relocation breadcrumb per the guiding principle above. Phase numbers freed by a relocation MAY be reused for new work on the same roadmap, because the cross-reference sweep eliminates lingering references to the old meaning. The decision rule: did the phase ever ship implementation? If yes → tombstone (deprecation). If no, and the work moved elsewhere → delete entry (relocation).

   **Migrate content first; deletion is the LAST step of relocation, not a shortcut.** When applying these rules to a legacy non-conforming doc that still carries unique live content (checkboxes, tracking detail, decisions, design rationale), migrate the content to its canonical new home FIRST. Use `git mv` so the rename/move is recorded as a single operation in history. Apply renumber/reorder/cleanup AT the new location once content is fully present there. Only delete the original entry once it carries no unique content not already preserved in the canonical home. This protects against the failure mode of treating a structural-cleanup pass as license to drop content that hasn't actually been migrated yet.

6. **Sub-letter notation is a narrow carve-out.** `phase{N}{a,b,c,...}_{descriptor}.md` is permitted ONLY for a single phase planned from the start as multiple atomic chunks shipping together as one body of work (e.g., a PoC `Phase 2a` + a Rollout `Phase 2b` planned together). The test: were both halves named at the same time, in the same planning pass, intended to ship as one initiative? If yes, sub-letter notation may be used. If a phase is added later as a retrofit, extension, or follow-on — even one that conceptually relates to an existing phase — append it as the next sequential phase number. **Do NOT add sub-letters retroactively** to express conceptual relationship; that conflates identity (sub-letter) with logical grouping (which belongs in roadmap prose).

7. **Each roadmap header includes a one-liner** noting the convention so a reader who sees Phase 10 above Phase 2 doesn't assume the file is broken. Suggested wording:

   > *Phases listed in logical rollout order. Phase numbers are creation-order identifiers and do not reflect rollout sequence; implementation order lives in [sprints.md](../../sprints.md).*

**Filename pattern (binding):**

```
phase{N}_{descriptor}.md          # canonical
phase{N}{a-z}_{descriptor}.md     # narrow carve-out per rule 6
```

Where `{N}` is a non-negative integer and `{descriptor}` is `snake_case`. No other phase-doc filename forms are valid (no unnumbered `phase_<name>.md`, no parenthetical disambiguation in filenames, no version suffixes). A CI lint enforcing `^phase[0-9]+[a-z]?_[a-z0-9_-]+\.md$` over `development/**/phase*.md` is the recommended guardrail.

**Why this rule exists:**

The previous convention was silent on what to do when a new phase needed to be inserted into an existing roadmap. Engineers (human and agent) defaulted to one of three failure modes:

- (a) reuse an existing phase number with a parenthetical descriptor (multiple "Phase 1" entries, distinguishable only by prose);
- (b) drop the number entirely (`phase_<name>.md`);
- (c) inject sub-letters retroactively, forcing renumbering of subsequent phases plus a cross-reference sweep across the corpus.

All three created a recurring cleanup cost. This rule eliminates the ambiguity by making phase number a mechanical identifier (count existing, add 1) and moving order-expressing concerns to `roadmap.md` (logical rollout order) and `sprints.md` (execution order). The 2026-05-08 `cluster_provision` and `networking` restructures were the trigger for this codification.

### Planning Folder Structure

Planning is organized by **component/concept**, not by abstract architectural layer. Each component has its own directory containing a `roadmap.md` and phase files.

**Planning folders (post-2026-05-07 restructure):**

1. **common/** — cross-cutting concerns owned by no single service. Component subfolders include `api/`, `bootstrap/`, `cluster_provision/`, `deploy-a-saurus/`, `django/`, `genesis/`, `harbor/`, `close_out/`, `networking/`, `resilience/`, `temporal/`. New cross-cutting concerns add a new `common/<component>/` subfolder.
2. **service/** — platform services with their own deployment lifecycle. Component subfolders include `1password/`, `argocd/`, `backups/`, `ceph/`, `github-automation/`, `inference/`, `monitoring/`, `secrets/`, `skyy-gate/`, `tailscale/`. Each service is a deployable artifact that ArgoCD or Temporal manages.
3. **workload/** — customer/product workloads (Synaptron, OpenClaw, Home Assistant, Docling). Each workload is a recipe + deployment target.
4. **skyy-net/** — future federation layer (multi-MDC orchestration).

**Historical note (2026-05-07 restructure):** earlier top-level domain folders `/development/infra/`, `/development/vm/`, `/development/container/` (the "six-domain" planning structure) have been collapsed:
- `/development/infra/` (Layer 1: physical hosts) absorbed into `/development/common/django/roadmap.md` Phases 4 + 5 — host orchestration is Django's job, the planning belongs there
- `/development/vm/` (Layer 2: VM lifecycle) absorbed into Django roadmap Phase 7 — VM lifecycle is similarly Django-orchestrated
- `/development/container/` (Layer 3) renamed to `/development/common/cluster_provision/` — was always cluster-provisioning planning, never container-runtime planning

The six-domain layer model (Architecture Standard §Two Dimensions of Desired State) still applies as the binding mental model for **the desired-state repo**, **the Helm chart library** (`skyy-command/deployments/<domain>/`), and **the Ansible collections** (`mdc-ansible-collections/<domain>/`). The PLANNING folder structure flattened to component-named for consistency with how the platform actually operates — every component has a roadmap that names what it does, not what layer it sits in.

**New planning folder placement rules:**
- Cross-cutting concern (touches multiple services or layers) → `/development/common/<component>/`
- Platform service with deployment lifecycle → `/development/service/<component>/`
- Customer-facing workload → `/development/workload/<name>/`
- Federation/multi-MDC concern → `/development/skyy-net/`

The planning structure does NOT dictate build order. Implementation order is determined by dependencies, revenue needs, and operational priorities — and is tracked in `sprints.md`, not in the planning directories.

## Cross-Roadmap Integration Pattern (binding)

**Rule (codified 2026-05-08):** when a platform service component (1Password, Vault, Harbor, Zabbix, etc.) lands in a sprint, **two distinct concerns must be planned separately**:

1. **Service deployment** — the service deploys as a standalone capability (Temporal workflows + SDK/API integration; ArgoCD-managed pod; per-service standards-conformance). Lives in the service's own roadmap (`/development/service/<service>/roadmap.md`). Lands first as its own sprint item.

2. **Django integration** — the service surfaces in the Django admin UI for operator-facing management (credential management, lifecycle ops, integration health, audit logs). Lives in the [Django Backend Roadmap](../../development/common/django/roadmap.md) as a phase or sub-phase. Lands separately, often a sprint or two later.

**Why separate:** services are USABLE without Django integration — Temporal workflows can call the service's SDK directly. Django integration adds operator convenience (admin UI for the service) but is rarely a hard prerequisite. Bundling integration with service deployment forces every service deployment to also block on Django UI work; separating them lets services land on their own timeline and Django integration batch multiple services together for efficiency.

**Default disposition:** services land standalone; Django integration is a SEPARATE Django-roadmap phase that batches multiple services together.

**Override:** if Django is REQUIRED for the service to function (rare — usually only when the service has no programmatic API and is admin-UI-driven by design), bundle integration at deployment time. The override must be justified in the service's roadmap Key Decisions block.

**Bidirectional cross-references:**
- The service roadmap names its corresponding Django-integration phase as a follow-up: *"Django integration tracked at [Django Backend Roadmap Phase X](../../common/django/roadmap.md)."*
- The Django roadmap phase cross-links back to the service roadmap: *"Couples to [Service Roadmap Phase Y](../../service/<service>/roadmap.md) — that roadmap owns the service-side."*
- Neither view is incomplete; both can find the other.

**Why this matters:** without the rule, Django integration leaks into service phase docs (because the service author thinks "I'll just add the admin UI here"), the service roadmap grows beyond its scope, the Django roadmap can't see what's coming, and integration work fragments across many service-specific phase docs that no one reads as a coherent Django-side trajectory. Codifying the rule makes "where does Django integration go" a 1-second decision instead of a per-service judgment call.

**Codified 2026-05-08** alongside the Django Backend Roadmap landing. Origin: Sprint 2-1c through 2-6 services were each accumulating "Django integration as a sub-phase" debt without a unified Django-side view; the Django roadmap consolidates that view; this rule enforces the structural separation going forward.

## Architectural Decisions — No ADRs

**The project does not use numbered ADR (Architecture Decision Record) artifacts.** Architectural decisions are recorded in one of two places:

1. **"Key Decisions" blocks inside a domain's `roadmap.md`** — for decisions scoped to that domain's phasing and design (e.g. `service/1password/roadmap.md §Key Decisions`). Preferred for single-domain decisions.
2. **New or amended standards in `standards/`** — for decisions that bind behavior across multiple domains or establish platform-wide invariants (e.g. Networking Standard, Tailscale Standard).

**Rationale — this choice is deliberate and AI-agent-driven:** the project is predominantly AI-agent-driven, not human-driven. Standards-docs and Key Decisions blocks present the **current, synthesized state** in one place per domain, which is what agents consume when they read documentation to plan or build. ADRs present decisions as an **append-only historical ledger** that requires readers to reconstruct current state by walking numbered files, detecting supersession, and synthesizing. That mismatches how agents read docs and would actively slow every planning and engineering run down. Human readers benefit equally — when you want the current rule you read the current rule, not 50 ADRs you have to synthesize yourself.

**Implications for planning docs and autonomous workflows:**

- When a planning doc (phase doc, roadmap, loose-ends entry) surfaces a decision as an *"ADR candidate"* it means "this decision is significant enough to warrant either a Key Decisions entry or a standards amendment" — it does **NOT** mean a separate ADR file will be created.
- Autonomous workflows (planner, architect, standards-architect, code-reviewer, etc.) may surface candidates in their review output but MUST NOT create standalone ADR files, propose a numbered-ADR convention, or use "ADR-blocked" as a blocking condition without translating it to "Key Decision candidate" or "standards amendment candidate." The home is either a roadmap's Key Decisions block or a standards amendment, selected by decision scope, landed through the interactive session per the Standards Governance rule.
- Commit messages for standards and roadmap edits must explain the **why** alongside the what, since the commit log serves as the project's durable decision-provenance record.

**Historical imports** (e.g. 1Password's `ADR-007` carried over from its source repo when planning docs were imported) are allowed as inline context — "was ADR-007 in source repo" — but are not treated as an active ADR numbering scheme in this repo.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Standards state the rule, never completion-state (binding)

A standard — or a Key Decisions block — states the **current binding rule**, and nothing about *where in the rollout* that rule is.

**Forbidden in a standard:** forward-looking completion/rollout state — `pending`, `not yet implemented`, `X will be Y`, `coming in Sprint N`, "the standard currently still says Z", or any status claim that goes stale the moment reality moves. Completion/rollout state lives in **planning docs** (roadmap / phase / sprint checkboxes), never in the standard.

**Why (binding rationale):** a standard that references state becomes *wrong* the instant the work lands or moves — a self-inflicted, perpetual maintenance burden that produces standard-vs-reality contradictions which mislead the next reader/engineer (cautionary example: the phase-10 doc kept asserting "the standard still says bake the driver" after the standard had been rewritten — the planning doc referencing the standard's *state* went stale, not the standard). **The standard says what MUST be true; the planning docs track whether it IS yet.**

**Acceptable:** a one-time **backward-looking provenance note** — `(corrected 2026-06-06)` — is a fixed historical fact, not a stale-prone status, and may stay.

**Distinct from stale cross-references:** when a policy *moves* and another standard still cites the old rule, that is a separate, unavoidable class — clean it when found. This rule prevents the *self-inflicted* state-references; it does not pretend cross-reference drift never happens. (Surfaced 2026-06-07.)

**`STUB` — the one permitted placeholder, and it is temporary.** The *only* content a standard marks as not-yet-stated is a rule that genuinely **cannot be planned yet** — one governing a system or decision that **conceptually does not exist yet** (not merely unimplemented — *unknowable* until the thing it governs takes shape). Mark that a clean `STUB`; do NOT invent a provisional rule, and do NOT add a "planned / locked / un-validated-against-code / planning-level" status banner (that is the same completion-state forbidden above, wearing a maturity hat). A *known* rule whose code simply isn't built yet is **stated as binding** — a spec is authoritative independent of its implementation; "the code isn't done" is never grounds to hedge the rule. The expectation: the **first engineer dispatch that needs a `STUB` flags the gap, and the rule is written at that moment.** A stub does not survive its first real use — it is temporary by definition. (Surfaced 2026-06-08.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Single-source codified fields — cite the block, don't re-list it (binding)

**Binding.** When a planning doc (roadmap / phase / sprint) needs the field set from a codified standard's **profile / schema block**, it MUST reference that block by citation — e.g. "the [§4.2 `workload-trusted` profile] block, verbatim" — and MUST NOT re-type the field list. The standard is the single source of truth; the doc **points, never copies** (DRY applied to the doc layer). This also applies to a standard's own exemplars: an exemplar that enumerates a schema's fields MUST carry the *complete* field set the code requires, so a lift-from-exemplar can't inherit a gap.

**Why (binding rationale):** a re-typed field list is a *second source of truth* that drifts silently — a one-field omission looks complete, almost matches the standard, and ships as a real gap. Three such drifts surfaced in the 3-7b suite alone: a `workload-trusted` inline list dropped `pod_security: restricted` → a cluster stood up with **no PSA enforcement** (caught only by holistic QC, after the four narrow reviewers each missed it); a phase-doc list conflated CSI `storage_classes` with node `vm_spec.storage`; and the §4.2 profile **exemplar itself** omitted the required `bridge` field.

**Where an inline enumeration is genuinely unavoidable:** gate it — a lightweight doc-conformance check (or reviewer-checklist item) that diffs the inline list against the standard's block, so a drift fails **loud** instead of relying on a reviewer noticing.

**Breaking it looks like:** a phase doc re-listing a standard's profile fields inline instead of citing the block; a standard exemplar missing a field the code requires; a codified field set duplicated into a doc with no conformance check reconciling the two. (Surfaced 2026-07-03, from three field-drift near-misses in the 3-7b suite.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Cross-ecosystem vendored standards — mirror/fork provenance (binding)

**Binding.** A separate-ecosystem repo (Algorithm-and-Sons, SkyyNet) that needs a standard this corpus already carries **copies it in — it does NOT live-reference the source repo** (a live cross-ecosystem link is an unversioned silent dependency, and a leak if the copying repo ever ships standalone; *"a little copying is better than a little dependency"*). Every vendored copy MUST carry, at the **top of the doc**, a provenance + intent flag:

> *Vendored from `<source repo/path>` on `<date>`. Intent: **MIRROR** (meant to track the source — a general change here is retrofitted back, and vice versa) | **FORK** (intentionally diverged for this ecosystem's context — the source is ancestry only, not a sync target).*

The flag is the **only** connective tissue — no back-reference, no automated sync. Its job is to force the question at edit time: *"does this change belong back in the source too (MIRROR), or is it specific to this ecosystem (FORK)?"* A general improvement to a MIRROR is retrofitted to the source in the same work; a FORK's divergence is expected and left. **Provenance points one way only — copy → source; the source repo never references the copy.**

**Why (binding rationale):** vendoring is deliberate — it buys each ecosystem the right to ship standalone, which is worthless if the copy silently drifts from a source it was *meant* to track (a MIRROR gone stale), or if a divergence that *should* exist gets "corrected" back into lockstep (a FORK mistaken for a pure copy). The flag makes the intended relationship explicit so drift is always a decision, never an accident — without re-introducing the live dependency the copy exists to avoid.

**Breaking it looks like:** a vendored standard with no provenance/intent flag; a copy that live-references the source (`../../mdc-master-planning/...`) instead of standing alone; a MIRROR-flagged copy edited with a general improvement that wasn't retrofitted to the source; or the source repo carrying a back-reference to a downstream copy. (Surfaced 2026-07-06 — the Documentation Standard is itself the first mirrored artifact.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Completion checkboxes — the check is the safeguard, not the typing (binding)

**Promoted out of § Sprint Tracking deliberately.** This is a repo-wide rule about planning artifacts generally, and it was nested inside the one section a consumer with no sprints excludes wholesale — so the exclusion swallowed it. **It survives any Sprint-Tracking exclusion.**

A **completion checkbox** — any `[ ]`/`[x]` asserting that work is done — is an **accountability claim, not a status field.** Its value is exactly the trust in whoever verified it.

**A dispatch MAY flip a checkbox for work delivered in its own diff.** The review stage **MUST verify every flip against the artifact — never against the run's account of it.**

- An **unverified flip is a finding.**
- A flip **for work not in the dispatch's own diff holds the PR** — the reviewer cannot check what it cannot see.
- **`sprints.md` remains human-only**, per § Sprint editing authority. It is the operator's cross-domain sequencing surface and no verification substitutes for that.

**Why this shape.** The protection the rule wants is *do not claim work that is not done*. A verifying reviewer delivers that; an operator flipping boxes they did not personally verify does not — and their flip carries **no verification record**, while the reviewer's does. **The mechanical act was never the safeguard.** This is `author ≠ judge` satisfied where it belongs: the judge checks the claim rather than performing the author's clerical work.

**The bar the reviewer is held to — built is not proven.** A checkbox marks work *demonstrated*, not work *written*. A requirement whose evidence does not yet exist stays **unchecked, with prose stating why**, even when its code has landed. A reviewer that flips on "the code is there" has not verified; it has read.

**Timing.** A flip for work delivered by a PR lands **with that PR**, and a planning doc on the default branch never marks complete a step whose code sits in an open one.

**Breaking it looks like:** a flip the reviewer did not check; a flip for work outside the dispatch's diff; a dispatch commit touching `sprints.md`; a requirement marked complete on the strength of code existing rather than evidence existing; a blanket pass that flips a group without per-item verification.

## Sprint Tracking

Sprint tracking lives in `development/sprints.md` and is the authoritative source for "what's being built when." Sprints pull specific phases from across domains into a **dependency-ordered backlog** — see the Sprint Model below.

### Sprint editing authority — human-in-the-loop only (binding)

`sprints.md` MUST NOT be edited without a human in the loop. It is the **exception** to the general planning-artifact rule: phase docs, `roadmap.md`, loose-ends entries, and epic breakdowns are dispatch-scope and MAY be edited by autonomous engineer runs — but the **sprint execution plan is not**. It is the operator's cross-domain sequencing surface, and every edit (new item, re-sequencing, checkbox flip, hour re-total) happens under human review.

Autonomous workflow dispatches and non-operator-reviewed sessions **surface** sprint-item candidates — they never write `sprints.md` themselves. A candidate discovered mid-dispatch (a new item, a re-order, a done checkbox) is raised in the PR body or a handoff for human-reviewed editing; it is **not** committed to `sprints.md` by the dispatch.

**Why:** the sprint plan is the operator's mental model of what is being built when. Uncontrolled edits from parallel sessions and engineer runs erode that model faster than any single edit improves it — the cost is the operator losing the thread, not one wrong line.

**Breaking it looks like:** an engineer dispatch or a non-human-reviewed session committing a new or edited `sprints.md` line; a checkbox flipped in `sprints.md` by an autonomous run without human sign-off; a new sprint item created by a dispatch instead of surfaced for human-reviewed insertion.

### Sprint Model — order by dependency; deviate consciously (binding)

Order the backlog by **dependency and gating** — the order the platform would be built in if nothing were skewed to run half-built in production (the `Depends on:` lines define it; common sense breaks ties). That order is the **default working order**; keep it honest to dependencies, not to urgency.

**Working out of order — pulling an item early, or building on a not-yet-ready dependency — is a conscious, logged choice that names the cost accepted** (rework debt, a half-built dependency). That is the operator deliberately swimming upstream for a specific reason (usually revenue) — **not** a reason to re-contort the backlog's order. Deviations are visible, deliberate exceptions; the order itself stays dependency-true. (The monthly `## Sprint N` buckets are capacity windows over this ordered backlog; the macro chain aligns with the [MDC Rollout Standard](../architecture/mdc_rollout_standard.md).)

### Sprint Structure

A sprint file organises work into sprints. **How a sprint is identified follows from what a sprint IS in that repo (binding)** — and the test is whether the identifier encodes something that moves.

**Time-boxed sprints are numbered.** Where a sprint is a *period* — `## Sprint 5 — August 2026 — VM Orchestration` — the ordinal encodes chronology, which does not reorder. Work inside is organised into **major steps** (`N-1`, `N-2`, `N-3`, …) and a trailing **close-out step**, always the last numbered item in the sprint.

> **⚠ MDC USED THIS MODEL AND NO LONGER DOES. Sprints in `development/sprints.md` are NAMED (binding, 2026-08-20).** Headings read `## Sprint — <name> (<hours>)`. **A new document that cites an MDC sprint by number is a defect**, and the number-to-name mapping for reading older documents lives in that file's own § *How things are named here*.
>
> **The trigger for the change is the one this section already named**, two paragraphs down: *"treat a suffix as a signal… if that happens repeatedly the sprints are behaving like components and the identification scheme should be revisited rather than patched."* **It fired twice and nobody read it.** MDC minted `Sprint 8a` / `Sprint 8b`, and separately re-cut the entire numbering on 2026-06-10 when a 6-sprint plan became 16 — a renumber cascade performed to insert work, which this section's own *Breaking it looks like* list already forbids.
>
> **The damage the delay caused, recorded because it is the argument for reading the signal early:** the re-cut left **~631 references** across 103 documents saying `Sprint N`, and because the numbering had been re-cut *once already*, a bare `Sprint 2` is now genuinely ambiguous between two different sprints in the same month. **Those cannot be mechanically corrected** — each needs a human to determine which numbering it meant. That cost is permanent and it is what numbering a thing that reorders actually buys.
>
> **Item ordinals (`2-4a`) inside MDC's sprint file are FROZEN LABELS, not live identifiers.** They encode a position in the pre-2026-06-10 structure and locate nothing today — ~1,193 references point at them, so they are kept as opaque stable names. **Do not mint new ones.**

**Component sprints are named, never numbered.** Where a sprint is *one thing being built*, sequenced by dependency, the ordinal encodes a judgement that changes as evidence arrives — so every reorder becomes a renumber plus a wave of stale cross-references, and the cost of acting on new evidence rises with the size of the plan. Headings read `## Sprint: <name>`, and items inside carry no ordinals.

**Why the axis is stated rather than one model asserted:** a repo whose sprints are components cannot conform to a numbering rule, because it is not building the same object. Numbering is safe exactly where the ordinal tracks something external and fixed; it is a liability where it encodes a decision the plan exists to revise.

**A numbered sprint's ordinal is immutable once assigned.** New work between existing sprints takes a **letter suffix** (`Sprint 8a`, `Sprint 8b`) rather than renumbering successors. Treat a suffix as a signal worth reading: it means the calendar and the ordinal have come apart, and if that happens repeatedly the sprints are behaving like components and the identification scheme should be revisited rather than patched.

**Breaking it looks like:** a numbered sprint whose ordinal has been changed; ordinals on items in a component-sprint file; a cross-reference to a sprint by number in a repo that reorders; a renumber cascade performed to insert work; **a new MDC sprint reference written as a number rather than a name; a newly-minted item ordinal in MDC's frozen `N-Mx` scheme; or a suffix (`8a`, `8b`) added a second time without re-reading the identification scheme it is a signal about.**

### What a sprint entry may contain (binding)

A sprint file's job is to be **scannable** — to answer "what is being built, and when" at a glance. Every rule here follows from that, and they bind regardless of which identification scheme above applies.

**A sprint plan is never a history lesson.** It states what is built or is going to be built, and nothing else. Why a decision was made, what an approach cost, what was tried and abandoned and on what reasoning — all of it belongs in the roadmap or the phase doc. An abandoned item is struck **there** with its explanation; it does not appear in the sprint file at all. Prose like *"used to be here but that didn't work"* is the shape to catch.

**An item names a thing that will exist.** Not a question to answer, not an argument for itself, not a citation of its evidence. *"Settle whether…"*, *"Resolve the…"*, *"Rule on…"* describe deliberation, not a deliverable — a sprint of them builds nothing and cannot be verified complete. This is distinct from the one-liner rule below: an item can be a single line and still name no artifact.

**Beware items that name an activity rather than an artifact.** They read as legitimate work and quietly become unbuildable when whatever the activity operated on changes — the item survives, its substrate does not, and nothing signals the gap.

**A delivered item carries its own stamp: `closed YYYY-MM-DD · ~Nh` (binding).** The closed date and the actual hours ride on the item itself, not in a changelog, a section header, or the commit that flipped it.

**This is the mechanism that makes *"never a history lesson"* affordable**, and it is why the two rules appear together. A sprint file can only afford to carry no history if the history is *already recorded somewhere durable* — the stamp is that record. Without it, `[x]` means *"this happened at some point, go read git"*, the file cannot be reorganised without losing when things landed, and the pressure to narrate history in the prose returns immediately because nothing else holds it.

The hours matter as much as the date: they are the only estimate-versus-actual signal the plan produces, and they cost nothing to record at the moment of closing and cannot be reconstructed later.

**Close-out is reopenable; delivered work is not (binding).** *"Did we ship it"* and *"did we finish tidying up"* are different questions, and only the second may be re-opened. When a closed sprint's tail work turns out to be unfinished, the **close-out item alone** returns to `[ ]` with a `reopened YYYY-MM-DD` stamp and the sprint header notes it — every delivered item stays `[x]`. Reopening delivered items to signal an unfinished tail destroys the shipped/not-shipped record, which is the one thing the checkboxes exist to hold.

Completion semantics are governed separately: a checkbox means shipped **and verified**, never attempted — see § Sprint Item Completion Gate below.

**Breaking it looks like:** a sprint item carrying rationale, alternatives, or a decision record; an item whose title poses a question; an entry describing an activity with no named artifact; an abandoned approach documented in the sprint file rather than struck in its phase doc; **a delivered item with no closed-date or hour stamp**; **a delivered item flipped back to `[ ]` because close-out reopened.**

### Sprint Item Completion Gate (binding)

**Binding.** Before flipping a sprint-item checkbox to `[x]`, the engineer in charge MUST run the `quality-control` agent against the completed work artifacts (PR diff for code work, phase doc for planning work) and dispose of every finding per the engineering-quality.md finding-disposition rule (fixed / rejected with reasoning / deferred with tracker). The checkbox represents "QC-pass complete," not "I think it's done." QC findings + their dispositions are posted to the sprint-item PR body or the sprint-review thread for audit trail.

**Evidence quality (binding).** When a test is cited as the evidence that an item is complete, that test MUST satisfy [Testing Standard § Test Efficacy](../development/testing/testing_standard.md) — demonstrably able to fail, proven by mutation. A completion mark whose evidence is a test that cannot fail records a protection that does not exist, and leaves no way to distinguish *fixed* from *never worked*. The checkbox inherits the strength of its evidence; hollow evidence makes the mark a claim rather than a record.

### Capability-Parity Gate for Rewrites & Ports (binding)

**Binding.** A sprint item that **replaces an existing implementation** — porting a behavior to new technology (bash→Temporal, Docker Compose→K8s, Chroniker→Temporal cron), rewriting a workflow, or otherwise superseding code already in operator use — MUST NOT be marked `[x]` until a **capability-parity audit** is recorded against the system being replaced:

1. **Enumerate** every behavior of the replaced implementation — not just the headline. Read the old code and list what it *actually did* (for a deploy script: image-update detection, health-check timeout loop, cleanup semantics, force-recreate path).
2. **Map each** to **ported** (cite where in the new system) or **consciously dropped** (named, with explicit operator sign-off + a one-line rationale).
3. **No silent drops.** A behavior that is neither ported nor signed-off-as-dropped is a parity gap that blocks completion. "The new code works and tests pass" is NOT the bar — "everything the replaced system did is ported, or the drop was a visible decision" is.

The audit lives as a `§Capability Parity` table in the rewrite item's phase doc — or, **for a service whose only planning artifact is a roadmap (no phase doc, e.g. monitoring), in that roadmap** — posted to the PR body / sprint-review thread alongside the QC dispositions.

**Why the binding:** three regressions surfaced in one 2026-06-02 session, all from "done" measured against "new code works" rather than parity — Vault Phase 1 marked CLOSED while production never cut over; the GitHub credential standard froze a bootstrap location as steady-state; and the Synaptron Phase-2 Temporal rewrite (Sprint 3-2b) silently dropped the Phase-0 `timpi_deploy.sh` auto-image-update capability the operator relied on. A parity table would have surfaced each at planning time. Sibling to the §Runtime Verification gate (which catches the inverse — a planning doc asserting behavior the running system does NOT have).

**Breaking it looks like:** a "port/rewrite/migrate X" item marked `[x]` with no §Capability Parity table in its phase doc; a parity table listing only the headline feature and omitting the secondary behaviors of the replaced code; a dropped capability with no operator sign-off recorded.

### Template-Conformance Gate for desired-state fields (binding)

**Binding.** A PR that adds or changes a field in a desired-state file MUST update that file's scaffold template (`skyy-command/templates/desired_state_templates/<domain>/`) in the same PR — per [Desired State Standard §5](../development/desired-state/desired_state_standard.md) + [Stateful Patterns §2.1](../development/temporal/stateful_patterns.md). The sprint item cannot be marked `[x]` otherwise. Sibling to the Capability-Parity Gate; same failure family — shipping against the letter of a standard while missing the steady-state shape it intends. **Cautionary example:** the 2026-06-04 Synaptron `image_ref` field added to the manifest without its template, which forced the adopt write-activity to insert the key at runtime and mis-place it.

**Breaking it looks like:** a desired-state field added/renamed with no matching scaffold-template change in the same PR; a write-activity that inserts a runtime key instead of updating a preset field (see [Stateful Patterns §2.4](../development/temporal/stateful_patterns.md)).

### Sprint Foundations Pattern (binding)

**Every sprint opens with a foundations cluster** — the work the rest of the sprint rests on, gathered first rather than scattered through it.

**The cluster is identified the way its sprint is** ([§ Sprint Structure](#sprint-structure)), and this is the part that was previously wrong: the rule was written as numbered-cluster machinery (`§N-1`, sub-items `N-1a`/`N-1b`) at a time when every sprint was numbered. **That contradicted § Sprint Structure's own rule that component sprints carry no ordinals**, leaving a repo with named sprints unable to conform to a binding section — not through omission, but because both rules could not be satisfied at once.

- **Numbered (time-boxed) sprints:** the cluster is the first major step, `### N-1. Sprint N Foundations (~hours)`.
- **Named (component) sprints:** the cluster is the first section, `### Foundations (~hours)`, with no ordinal.

**Convention:**

- The heading is fixed across sprints of the same kind
- The cluster preamble paragraph names the foundational items inside (1Password deployment, Cluster 2 standup, dual-resolver elimination, etc.) and explains why they're foundational to the rest of the sprint
- **Numbered sprints:** sub-items follow the `N-1a`, `N-1b`, … format with descriptive titles, and new foundational items land as further sub-letters (`N-1f`, `N-1g`, …) **without renumbering existing items**
- **Named sprints:** sub-items carry descriptive titles and no ordinals; new foundational items are simply appended. **The sub-letter machinery exists solely to avoid renumbering — a scheme with no numbers has nothing to protect and MUST NOT invent ordinals to imitate one**

**Examples (post-2026-05-07 sprint restructure):**
- `Sprint 2-1` "Sprint 2 Foundations" — bundles Temporal worker segmentation + service exposure foundation + 1Password deployment + Django foundations (dual-resolver elimination + standards sweep)
- `Sprint 3-1` "Sprint 3 Foundations" — K3s Cluster 2 standup (Cluster 2 IS the Sprint 3 foundation; everything else in the sprint depends on it)
- `Sprint 4-1` "Sprint 4 Foundations" — SkyyGate Phase 1 Temporal deployment (every later SkyyGate sub-item depends on the Phase 1 substrate)
- `Sprint 5-1` "Sprint 5 Foundations" — verification of upstream-sprint deliverables that Sprint 5's main work depends on
- `Sprint 6-1` "Sprint 6 Foundations" — Zabbix configuration-as-code automation (downstream Ceph + monitoring work depends on it)

**Why the convention:**
- **No renumbering when foundations grow.** Adding 2-1f and 2-1g (Django foundations) to Sprint 2-1 didn't renumber existing 2-1a through 2-1e. New foundational concerns just get the next sub-letter.
- **"Where do prerequisite items go" is a 1-second decision.** Anything foundational lands in §N-1; sprint-internal sub-step ordering happens via sub-letter sequencing.
- **Reader entering a sprint sees foundations FIRST.** The numbering matches the dependency order — §N-1 is what unblocks everything else.

**Forbidden:**
- ❌ Section title that describes specific content rather than the foundations role (e.g., "1Password deployment to Cluster 1") — descriptive content lives in the cluster preamble + sub-items, not the section title
- ❌ Foundational work in §N-2 or later when it could have lived in §N-1 — foundational work goes first, period
- ❌ "Sprint N Loose Ends" or similar misfit-toy titles — that is the trailing close-out step, not §N-1

**Trailing close-out tracker** (separate concern): every sprint's last major-step section is its close-out tracker (e.g., `2-8 Sprint 2 close-out`) — it tracks the sprint's recurring end-of-sprint checks (see the closure criteria below).

### Major Steps and Sub-Items

Each major step is a `### N-M. Title (~hours)` heading. Within a major step, sub-items track distinct deliverables:

```markdown
### 1-2. DAS Phase 1 + Version-of-Record Phase A (~30 hrs)
**Domain:** common/deploy-a-saurus Phase 1 + version-of-record Phase A

[One paragraph describing the scope]

- [ ] **1-2a DAS Phase 1 complete** ([phase1_temporal_workflows.md](...)) — brief description
- [ ] **1-2b DAS version-of-record Phase A** ([das_version_of_record_design.md](...)) — brief description

**Depends on:** [dependencies]
```

**Sub-item format rules:**
- Numbering is hierarchical: `1-1a`, `1-1b`, `2-5a`, `2-5b` (sprint-major_step-sub_item)
- **The sub-letter is mandatory on every work item.** Even when a major step has exactly one work item, that item is named with the `a` sub-letter (`4-6a`, `1-5a`), never the bare major-step identifier (`4-6`, `1-5`). Reasons: (a) consistent identifier shape across all items; (b) adding a second sub-item later doesn't trigger renaming the first; (c) legacy loose-end identifiers trace via sub-letter, so every work item must have one.
- Title is **inside** the bold: `**1-2a Title here**` — not `**1-2a** — Title here`
- Each sub-item links to its phase doc. If no phase doc exists, flag it: `(NEEDS PLANNING — phase_doc_name.md to be written by planning engineer)`
- Sub-items are **one-liners** — the sprint doc is scheduling + scope, not implementation detail. That detail lives in the phase doc.
- When a major step has only one body of work, it still gets one sub-item line with the link + description. Don't leave a major step with zero sub-items.
- **Adding sub-items to an existing major step uses the next unused letter (binding).** When new scope is added to a major step that already has sub-items, the new item gets the NEXT UNUSED letter — NOT a sub-fork of an existing letter (`b.5`, `b'`, `b-prime`, etc.) and NOT a renumbering of existing items. The "no renumbering when foundations grow" principle from §Sprint Foundations applies to every major step, not just `§N-1`. **Pre-flight verify:** before assigning a new sub-letter, grep `sprints.md` for the proposed identifier to confirm it's unused. **Why:** sub-letters are IDENTITY, not ordering — once assigned, the identifier is stable. Late-arriving scope that logically slots between existing items still takes the next unused letter (assignment order, not topological order); prose ordering within the major step expresses logical sequence, not the letter sequence. **Worked example:** when 1P Phase 2's Sprint 2-4 slot was assigned 2026-05-13 (PR #48), Sprint 2-4 already had 2-4a (security audit) + 2-4b (API-key validation) + 2-4c (aggregator). The new item correctly took **2-4d** — NOT 2-4b' or 2-4b.5. 1P Phase 2 work logically belongs between 2-4a and 2-4c (pre-aggregator), but the identifier letter is assignment-order, not logical-order; the major step's prose expresses the logical sequence.

### (NEEDS PLANNING) Convention

When a sprint item references a phase doc that doesn't exist yet, the sub-item carries `(NEEDS PLANNING)` in place of the link. The planning engineer writes the phase doc before engineer runs begin on that item.

```markdown
- [ ] **1-3a k3s-1 Provision** (NEEDS PLANNING — `phase1_k3s-1_provision.md` to be created)
```

This makes it immediately visible which sprint items are ready for engineer execution and which need planning work first.
