## Deferred Work — SUPERSEDED (binding)

> **⚠ This section's GitHub-Issues rule is superseded by the [Tracked Items Standard](./tracked_items_standard.md) (2026-08-25).** Deferred work now lives in **`tracked/issues/`**, one file per item, alongside three sibling stores — the standup tracker, research candidates, and standards candidates. **GitHub Issues are retired for tracked work; no new one is filed.**
>
> **What survives unchanged, and is the durable half:** the placement order below, the prohibition on a second surface, and the retirement-residue rule. Only the *destination* changed.

Deferred work lives in **exactly one surface**. A second surface always becomes the ungoverned one, and work drifts to it because filing there is cheaper than planning.

**The Loose Ends Convention is retired, and its store is gone.** All 139 open items in `development/common/loose_ends/` were dispositioned into phase-doc checkboxes and the 13 `sprint_N_loose_ends.md` files deleted on 2026-08-07. **Recreating that directory, or any per-sprint carried-work ledger like it, is a violation of this section rather than a fallback when placement is hard** — a store that accepts anything is how 139 items accumulated across nine files, eight of which never had a single item triaged out. The evergreen close-out checklist moved to `development/common/close_out/sprint_end_recurring.md`; it holds recurring checks, never carried items.

#### Retiring a tracking surface requires a residue sweep (binding)

Removing a tracking surface — this store, a ledger file, any artifact actors were told to write into — is not complete when its items are placed. **Deleting the artifact does not delete the instruction to rebuild it, and the instruction is the durable part.** An actor that reads "record it in X" and finds no X will create X, correctly believing it is following the rule.

Two sweeps, both required before the removal merges:

1. **References** — links and paths that now dangle. Mechanical, and the one everyone remembers.
2. **Instructions** — every place that *directs* an actor to write into the surface: standards, prompts, rules, agent definitions, checklists, phase-doc boilerplate. **This is the larger surface and the one that reopens the hole.** Search for the concept, not just the path — an instruction usually names the thing, not its location.

**The removal is gated on both reaching zero, in the same merge.** Draining first and cleaning up afterwards leaves a window in which the surface is gone and the instruction to recreate it still stands.

**Breaking it looks like:** a retired surface reappearing because a prompt or rule still names it; a deletion PR that fixed links but left a numbered step saying "record deferred gaps in \<surface\>"; a residue sweep that grepped only the file path.

### Filing authority

**No autonomous dispatch may file deferred work as an issue.** A build or planning run that discovers deferred work surfaces it in its own report and stops there; the PR-review stage triages what was surfaced and files what qualifies. Humans and human-reviewed sessions may open issues at any time.

**This constrains one operation, not the surface.** The rule governs an issue that *removes* something from a run's deliverable — work the run could have done, recorded elsewhere so its output reads as complete. It does not govern an issue that *is* the deliverable: a no-change outcome where the run produced no work product and the issue is the entire result — a planning STOP on insufficient inputs ([Research §5](../development/research/research_standard.md)), a `research-candidate` with nowhere yet to live ([Research §7](../development/research/research_standard.md)). Nothing is being excluded there, because there is nothing to exclude.

The asymmetry is also one of visibility: a false no-change outcome is loud — no plan was produced, and the operator sees that immediately — while a buried deferral is quiet, because the PR still reads as clean. The gate exists for the quiet one.

**Why the reviewer and not the discoverer:** a run that can file its own deferrals has a disposal chute for its own scope — file it, move on, the PR looks clean. The reviewer has nothing to offload, because it is never the party that would otherwise do the work. Concentrating filing in one actor also makes miscalibration correctable in one place.

### A finding about the work in hand never reaches placement (binding)

**Answer this before the placement ladder below, because a finding about the work in hand is not deferred work at all — it is current work, and the ladder's every rung routes outward.**

For a finding about the work in hand, exactly three dispositions exist:

| Disposition | When |
|---|---|
| **fixed** | corrected in the change that produced the finding |
| **rejected** | not a real defect — stated with the reasoning that makes it not one |
| **hold** | real and not fixed here: a correction pass fixes it, or a human rules on it |

**There is no fourth, and the absence is the rule.** Not discouraged, not permitted with a good pointer — a container is simply not among the available answers. A criterion that says *prefer not to file* loses to the arithmetic every producing run is under: **filing costs one line and fixing costs the rest of the budget**, so any exit that is reachable and looks legitimate gets taken. The exit has to be absent, not narrow.

**`rejected` is retained deliberately.** A finding about one's own work genuinely can be wrong, and forcing a fake fix is worse than a reasoned rejection. It is the one place a run could still hide, and that is accepted against the alternative.

**What counts as the work in hand:**

- an artifact the change **created or edited** — *including one it created correctly but incompletely*
- a commit made **to unblock** the change
- **output the change produced** that does not conform to a rule binding it

***"I noticed X while doing Y"* is not enough.** The question is whether X is part of Y.

**The one carve-out, stated so it does not become the new exit.** If the owning work has **already merged**, it cannot be given a runway; route it to whatever is next touching that artifact. A new container is legitimate **only** when no open work owns it — and *"the owner merged"* is a fact stated, not a conclusion reached because fixing looked expensive.

#### Every finding names the artifact it is about (binding)

This is the half that makes the rule a check rather than an exhortation. **A finding states the file or artifact it concerns.** Ownership is then **computed, not judged**: a finding whose artifact appears in the change's own diff has three dispositions available and no others.

Without it, "related to the work in hand" is a judgement made by the party with an incentive to judge it loosely — which is the same defect as [§ Placement](#placement--phase-checkbox-first-issue-second-binding)'s title-versus-body rule, one layer up. **A finding with no named artifact cannot be routed and is itself a finding.**

**Where findings are typed, the field is added additively and its conformance check follows in a later pass.** A required-field change applied mid-flight routes every already-conforming run to a human, which produces silence rather than an error — the opposite of the intent.

**Breaking it looks like:** an issue filed against the change that produced the finding; a finding about an artifact in the change's own diff routed to a phase checkbox, a candidate row, or any other container; a finding with no artifact named; *"the owner merged"* asserted rather than checked; an incompletely-created artifact treated as someone else's problem because the part that exists is correct.

### Placement — phase checkbox first, issue second (binding)

**0. Is it a PROPOSAL — capability that does not exist yet and would be added?** Then it goes to [`standards/architecture/research/candidates.md`](../architecture/research/candidates.md) and is **NEVER an Issue, however clean its done-state.**

**This question comes first because the tests below route proposals wrongly.** A proposal answers *"nothing is broken"* to the defect test and *"yes, it is buildable"* to the done-state test — so every proposal qualifies, and the tracker fills with capability requests indistinguishable at a glance from live defects. An Issue says *something is wrong*; a proposal says *something could be better*. A queue that holds both is a queue nobody can triage quickly.

**Bias toward `candidates.md` when a finding reads either way.** The costs are asymmetric: a proposal misfiled as an Issue silts a surface triaged every morning; a defect misfiled as a candidate waits until the next planning pass. One is daily noise, the other is a delay.

**Who may write it, and why that is not the filer.** A **producing run MAY append its own proposals** to `candidates.md`, in its own PR, with `decision` left **blank** — blank means untriaged, and `decision` is the planning pass's output alone. The review stage then **verifies the row exists** and treats surfaced-but-not-placed as a fix-in-place hold.

**This is a deliberate exception to § Filing authority, and it is scoped to proposals only.** That rule exists because a run that can file its own deferrals has a disposal chute for its own scope — file it, move on, the PR looks clean. **That reasoning does not reach a proposal:** a proposal is capability that does not exist, so by construction it was never work the run was asked to do and never scope it could be dodging. The asymmetry the rule rests on is absent, and the authority that matters is retained — the reviewer still rules on whether the *classification* was right, and holds the PR if a proposal was a defect in disguise.

**The mechanism is why this had to be said.** Naming an actor as a surface's writer is not sufficient; the actor must be **able to write it by the mechanism that surface requires.** An **API** surface — a GitHub Issue, a PR comment — needs only a token, so any run can write one, including a decide-only reviewer. A **file** surface needs an edit, a commit and a push, so only a run that produces a PR can write it. `candidates.md` is a file. **A decide-only reviewer structurally cannot place a proposal**, so routing proposals to a file while naming only the reviewer as filer produces a correctly-classified finding that no actor can place — it survives in a PR body and dies at merge, which is the exact failure this bucket was created to prevent.

> **⚠ This constraint WIDENED on 2026-08-25 and is now the sharpest open question in the tracked-item design.** The [Tracked Items Standard](./tracked_items_standard.md) retires GitHub Issues, so **all four stores are file surfaces.** The API escape hatch this paragraph describes — *"needs only a token, so any run can write one, including a decide-only reviewer"* — **no longer exists for any store.** A decide-only reviewer can now place nothing at all. **Resolving that is a `claude-dot-files` question** (commit to the branch under review, harvest a structured block from the comment, or grant a narrow write), and until it is resolved, **a review-stage finding still dies at merge.** Surfaced to the architecture session 2026-08-25.

**`standards/architecture/research/` is a WORKING SURFACE, not curated binding product.** Queues and evidence — `candidates.md`, research papers, syntheses — are appended by the runs that generate them. Standards-governance's human-in-the-loop rule binds the *curated* standards corpus and does not reach this directory. The rulings inside it stay human: a candidate's `decision` and a direction row's `status` are set by the planning pass and the operator respectively, never by a producing run.

**Breaking it looks like:** an Issue proposing capability that does not exist; an Issue whose remedy begins "adopt", "introduce", "build a" with nothing currently failing; a proposal filed because it had a clean done-state.

**Before** the qualification test below, answer two placement questions, in order. Both default **against** a new issue: the issue queue has the lowest filing cost of any surface, so it is the one that silts up first, and every item on it consumes an operator disposition at every standup until it closes.

**1. Does it have a done-state today?** An item whose remedy waits on a **named trigger**, or on a system **not yet built or still in progress**, cannot be closed — only carried. A carried issue reads as neglect on every standup while being structurally unable to move, and the anti-rot flag misfires on it. Such an item belongs as a **checkbox on the phase that owns the trigger**, where its readiness and its parent's readiness are the same event.

**Assume the checkbox fits; file an issue only when it demonstrably does not.** The order matters — evaluated the other way round, everything looks issue-shaped, because an issue accepts anything.

**2. Is it closely related to something that already exists?** Then it is an **expansion of that item**, not a sibling. Two entries describing one concern cost two dispositions, two reviews, and eventually two PRs contending over the same files while the second author re-derives the first's decisions. Expand the existing item — its title, its body, its checkbox list — rather than opening a neighbour.

Neither question relaxes the rule below: **an item small enough to fix in place is still fixed in place**, not filed anywhere. These questions decide *where a filed item lives*, not *whether small work gets recorded*.

**The placement decision is made from the item's body, never its title.** Titles state a consequence and therefore read alike across very different items; two that look like the same concern routinely are not, and one that looks blocked routinely is not.

### Four more ways an item already has a container (binding)

The two questions above catch the common cases. These four were each measured on a real mis-filed item, and each defaults **against** a new issue.

**3. Is this the same MECHANISM as an existing issue, in different code?** Then it is one concern with two instance sites — expand the existing item. **Search by mechanism, not by keyword.** Two entries can describe one defect and share no vocabulary at all; a keyword search will never connect them, and ruling on them separately risks two different answers to one architectural question. Ask *"what would fix both?"* — if the answer is one decision, it is one item.

**4. Does any phase own this area at all?** If nothing does, **the missing planning home IS the finding** — surface that, do not file the instance. Question 1 says *assume the checkbox fits*, but a checkbox needs a phase doc to sit on; with no owner, the queue absorbs the item by default and the cause goes unrecorded. An item that is future sprint scope rather than discrete deferred work belongs to whoever owns the plan, not to the tracker.

**5. Does it belong to a standard's owner?** A gap, contradiction or missing clause in a standard is **routed to that standard's owner and codified**, never tracked. Filing it converts a decision someone can make today into an item that survives standups unresolved.

**6. Did this same pass already surface it, in the same file or function?** One pass, one concern, one entry. Two defects in one function filed separately cost two dispositions, two reviews, and eventually two changes contending over the same lines.

**And when re-checking an existing deferral, verify its PREMISE, not just its pointer.** "Open it and confirm the item is there" is satisfied by a pointer whose underlying assumption has been reversed — an item deferred as *"already scheduled"* after a ruling cancelled the schedule resolves perfectly and means nothing. If the premise is dead, re-open the item; do not file a new one beside it.

**Prior art lives in every repo the work spans.** In a multi-repo platform an item's home is frequently in a sibling repo — planning items in the planning repo, code items in the code repo. *"No existing item covers this"* concluded from one repo's tracker is not a finding, it is an unfinished search.

**Breaking it looks like:** two issues whose remedies are the same decision; an issue filed for an area no phase owns, with no note that none does; a standards gap in the tracker; two entries from one pass over one function; a deferral re-confirmed by opening its pointer without re-reading what it assumed.

### Qualification

An item qualifies as an issue only if **all three** hold:

1. It is unrelated to the work in hand — decided by the artifact test in [§ A finding about the work in hand never reaches placement](#a-finding-about-the-work-in-hand-never-reaches-placement-binding), not by impression.
2. It is substantial in size or effort.
3. It is not already covered by an existing sprint item or phase.

Anything failing (2) is fixed in place rather than filed — the substantial bar exists to protect the planning pipeline, not the issue queue.

### Disposition (binding)

**An issue MUST NOT survive a standup in the same state.** At every standup each open issue reaches one of four dispositions:

1. **Resolved now** — acting costs less than scheduling it.
2. **Scheduled** — routed into an existing sprint item or phase (PM3 + operator).
3. **Planned** — the issue exposes a hole in what is currently planned; new planning and sprint items are created for it.
4. **Closed as invalid** — the item does not qualify. This is **feedback to the tool that filed it**; a pattern of invalid issues is evidence of a miscalibrated reviewer and is acted on as a tooling defect, not as cleanup.

Kicking the can is not a disposition, and neither is acknowledging an item and leaving it open. An issue that cannot move is blocked — the blocker is the real item and gets its own disposition.

**Breaking it looks like:** an autonomous dispatch filing its own deferred work as an issue; a new entry added to a `sprint_N_loose_ends.md` file; an issue carried across two consecutive standups with no disposition; deferred work recorded only in a PR body, a run reflection, or a code comment; **an issue whose remedy waits on a named trigger or an unbuilt system** (that is a phase checkbox — it has no closable state); **two or more issues describing one concern** (the second is an expansion of the first); **a placement or fold decision made by reading titles rather than bodies.**

## The Standup Tracker (binding)

A single, permanent GitHub issue titled **`standup-tracker`** on `mdc-master-planning` is the platform's **operating agenda** — where we left off, what is unresolved, and what that means for how today gets tackled. It is read at the start of every standup, before the issue and PR sweep, as the frame the sweep lands inside.

**It is not deferred work, and the § Deferred Work rules above do not govern it.** It borrows the GitHub-issue *mechanism* because that mechanism fits a document edited daily by several sessions — one API call, no branch, no commit ceremony, no merge conflict on the artifact least able to afford one. The semantics are its own.

### What distinguishes it from the other surfaces

| Surface | Holds | Lifecycle |
|---|---|---|
| **Sprint** | planned development work, sequenced by dependency | items close; the plan persists |
| **Issue** | one discrete unit of deferred work with a proposed action | filed → dispositioned → **closed** |
| **Standup tracker** | operating state and next moves | **never closes**; items are **pruned** |

An issue has a definable done-state. The tracker carries **state that needs carrying** — which is why it has an exit the issue taxonomy cannot express: an item that reached resolution is **removed** roughly a week later, because it stopped being agenda. That is curation, not disposition.

### What belongs in it

1. **Work that is blocked on something else happening first** — the blocker is the item; the tracker records what is waiting behind it.
2. **Work outside the sprint entirely** — live operations, fleet incidents, one-off platform tasks that were never development work and never will be.
3. **Continuity** — a multi-day operation's current position, so a session boundary does not lose it.

**Only what is NOT derivable from another surface.** The standup already sweeps open issues, open PRs, and recently-merged work. Anything the tracker restates from those will drift and rot. It holds the irreducible remainder.

Anything with a clean done-state and a proposed action is an **issue**, not a tracker line. Anything that is planned development work is a **sprint item**. The tracker is what neither of those can hold.

### Rules (binding)

- **The disposition obligation binds each LINE, not the issue.** Every unresolved item is considered at every standup and either acted on, re-stated with what changed, or explicitly carried with the reason it cannot move. "The tracker was reviewed" is not a disposition — that is the exact non-attendance failure that killed the loose-ends convention, relocated one level up.
- **Every item carries three ORTHOGONAL flags.** They are independent and must not be collapsed into one axis:
  - **`status`** — `ready` / `not-ready`. **Permission to act**, and **only the operator sets it.** This is not a fact about blockedness; an item can be entirely unblocked and still `not-ready` because it is not its turn. This flag is the admission-control surface for what the fleet works on — without it, an actor could derive "unblocked" for itself and start anything.
  - **`state`** — `blocked` / `queued` / `in-progress` / `resolved`. Where the item sits in completion.
  - **`ownership`** — who has claimed it, or `unassigned`.

  The combinations carry meaning the flags cannot carry alone: `ready + queued + unassigned` is available to claim; `ready + blocked` is pre-authorised and starts the moment the blocker clears; **`not-ready + in-progress` is a detectable violation** — work in flight that was never authorised.

- **Resolved items are pruned.** Setting `state: resolved` MUST be accompanied by a **`resolved: YYYY-MM-DD`** stamp; the item is deleted at the first standup **≥14 days** after that date. The stamp is what makes pruning mechanical rather than a guess at a line's age — an item without one cannot be pruned, and that is deliberate. The delay exists so a resolution that proves **wrong** is still visible and re-openable. A tracker that grows month over month is failing; items are meant to flow through it.
- **Maintained in the standup**, by the operator and the PM session together. **No autonomous dispatch writes to it** — same boundary as issue-filing authority, and for the same reason.
- **It is never a deferral target.** An item parked "on the tracker" to get it out of a run's deliverable is a laundered deferral; deferrals point at scheduled work or work in motion, per § Deferred Work.

### Forward compatibility — agent-readable work assignment

The tracker is the intended substrate for the autonomous-development model the harness is being built toward: an agent asking *"what is ready, and which of it is mine?"* Items should therefore be written so **readiness and ownership are legible** — what unblocks a blocked item, and who or what would pick it up. That capability is not built; the shape is chosen now so the tracker does not have to be rewritten to acquire it.

**Breaking it looks like:** a second tracker issue; the tracker used as a deferral target; an autonomous dispatch editing it; a standup that acknowledges the tracker without ruling on its lines; a resolved item with no `resolved:` date stamp; resolved items accumulating past the prune window; a tracker line that duplicates an open issue or a sprint item.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sprint Close-Out (binding)

**Close-out is a VERIFICATION GATE, not a work phase — and this is the change most likely to be missed.** It was historically the sprint's resolution stage: findings accumulated into a per-sprint loose-ends ledger through the sprint and were worked off at the end, which is why close-out carried real hours. **That store is retired** ([§ Deferred Work](#deferred-work--github-issues-binding)) and findings are now placed *at discovery* — a phase checkbox, an expansion of an existing item, or an issue. **Nothing accumulates for close-out to work off.**

So close-out no longer resolves anything; it **confirms** that nothing was left unplaced. A close-out step still sized like a work phase is a leftover from the ledger era and should be re-sized to what verification actually costs.

**The whole of close-out is ONE checkbox and two conditions.** A sprint's last step closes when both hold:

1. **The repo's recurring close-out checks have been run for this sprint, and every finding they produced is dispositioned** — fixed, rejected with reasoning, or placed ([§ Deferred Work](#deferred-work--github-issues-binding)).
2. **No open issue belongs to work this sprint covered.** An issue that should have entered this sprint's planning and did not is an *unclosed sprint*, not a carried-forward item.

**The recurring-check list is per-repo; this standard requires that one exist, not which one.** MDC's is [`common/close_out/sprint_end_recurring.md`](../../development/common/close_out/sprint_end_recurring.md) — **that file is the instance, not the requirement.** A repo supplies its own list and is conformant; adding entries to it needs no amendment here. Never duplicate the list into a per-sprint doc — reference it. It is a recurring-checks checklist, **never a ledger of carried work.**

**One accountability checkbox, never per-item.** It must assert *both* conditions and must make **dispositioned** visibly distinct from **run** — the entire reason it exists is that "we ran the checks" and "we read the output" are different claims, and only the second closes a sprint. Minimum form:

```markdown
- [ ] **Sprint close-out** — recurring checks run for this sprint and every finding
      dispositioned (fixed / rejected-with-reasoning / placed); no open issue belongs
      to this sprint's work.
```

**Size it as verification.** One checkbox over a list that is already written is not a work package, and a close-out step carrying work-phase hours is a leftover from the ledger era.

**Breaking it looks like:** per-item close-out checkboxes; a close-out marked complete with findings run but undispositioned; a close-out step sized in the tens of hours; a per-sprint copy of the recurring list; the recurring list accumulating carried work; a sprint closed while an open issue covers work it was responsible for.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## User Guide (operator manual)

User-facing operator documentation — installation instructions, hardware requirements, internal/customer deployment guides, integration walkthroughs, networking reference — lives at `mdc-master-planning/guide/`, **not** in any application repo. One canonical home for everything operators read.

### Rules

- **Location:** `mdc-master-planning/guide/` — every markdown file a human reads as a manual.
- **Name:** `guide/`. **Not** `docs/`, **not** `official_documentation/`, **not** `manual/`, **not** `user_docs/`. One name, no synonyms.
- **Organization:** top-level numbered sections for stable ordering (`01. Table of Contents`, `02. Getting Started`, `03. Requirements`, `04. Infrastructure`, `05. Services`, `06. Workloads`, ...). Sub-entries use alphabetic prefixes (`a.`, `b.`, `c.`) for within-section ordering.
- **Six-domain naming for domain-specific sections (binding).** Section names for domain-specific content follow the platform's six-domain vocabulary used across `skyy-command/deployments/`, `desired-state-<mdc>/container/k3s-<N>/`, `mdc-ansible-collections/`, and `development/`: `04. Infrastructure` (← `infra/`), `05. Services` (← `service/`), `06. Workloads` (← `workload/`). Meta sections (`02. Getting Started`, `03. Requirements`, `11. Troubleshooting`, `12. Archive`) keep operator-task names because they don't map to a six-domain folder. Reduces cognitive load — same concept, same word, everywhere.
- **One file per service (binding).** Per-service operator runbook content lives in a SINGLE file at the appropriate domain section (e.g., `05. Services/<service>.md`, `06. Workloads/<workload>.md`). The file is organized by lifecycle stage: deployment first, then post-deploy operation, common commands, troubleshooting, rotation procedures, etc. — all as sections within the same file. **Do not split per-service content across multiple directories** (e.g., a separate `06. Operations/<service>.md` while deployment lives in `05. Services/<service>.md`). Operators reach for the SERVICE, not the lifecycle-stage; a service is a cohesive unit. Splitting adds cognitive load + cross-reference proliferation without compensating benefit.
### Guide architecture — section purpose, ordering, and prerequisite placement (binding, ratified 2026-07-26)

- **`02. Getting Started` sub-docs have defined purposes — the discriminator is the TENANCY-vs-ARTIFACT test.** `c. Installation Guide` is the **ORDERED standup sequence** — "do this THEN this THEN this"; it is what lets someone bring up a new MDC correctly without jumping around and playing chicken-and-egg games. **`b.` holds TENANCY acquisition; `c.` Prerequisites holds ARTIFACT provisioning.** *Tenancy* = the account/tenant itself — has procurement/approval **lead time** and **outlives any single standup** (a GitHub account, a 1Password Business subscription, a Tailscale tailnet, a Cloudflare account, the physical substrate). *Artifacts* = the tokens, vaults, Service Accounts, and OAuth clients **minted WITHIN a tenancy** — they carry expiry and are created **close to the moment of use and verified immediately before consumption**, placed in `c.` at their dependency point. The two pressures point opposite directions and apply to different things: surface long-lead-time work EARLY (tenancy), mint credentials JUST-IN-TIME (artifacts) — the tenancy/artifact line is exactly where those pressures separate. Exemplar shape: Tailscale = tailnet in `b.`, OAuth client in `c.`; 1Password = account in `b.`, vault set + SAs in `c.`; GitHub = account in `b.`, PATs in `c.`.
- **The split carries NO correctness job — do not re-add ordering semantics to it.** Dependency correctness across the whole guide (read as one sequence) is owned entirely by the no-forward-references rule below, independent of which doc a step lives in. The `b.`/`c.` split is purely organizational. This is *why* ordering-based placement tests ("outside the standup process," "no ordering dependency") cannot discriminate — ordering dependencies are transitive and effectively universal, so such tests justify any placement; they are retired, not the rule.
- **Ordering-dependency rule (binding).** Any step whose correctness depends on *when* it happens relative to standup belongs in the ordered doc (`c.`), positioned **at its dependency point** — never in `b.`, never in a downstream service section.
- **No forward references (binding — mechanically auditable).** A guide step MUST NOT reference an artifact (vault, token, account, OAuth client, file) the guide has not yet told the operator to create. Audit mechanically: walk the guide in reading order and flag every referenced artifact with no prior creation step — a doc-manager AUDIT pass can run this check verbatim.
- **Prerequisite co-location.** Operator out-of-band setup (accounts, vaults, tokens, OAuth clients) lands in a prerequisites block **at first use, in dependency order** — NOT filed under the service that consumes it. The owning service doc keeps the canonical detailed procedure and is **referenced, not duplicated** (single source of truth: one canonical home plus pointers).

**Breaking it looks like:** a guide step referencing a vault/token/account the reader was never instructed to create; operator setup for service X buried in service X's deployment doc when it must happen before standup; an ordering-dependent step sitting in `b. Pre-configuration`; or the same operator prerequisite documented in two places instead of one canonical home plus pointers.

- **Assets:** images, diagrams, and other binary references live under `mdc-master-planning/guide/assets/`. Reference them with relative paths from the markdown.
- **Internal links** between guide entries use relative paths rooted at `guide/` — e.g. `guide/02. Getting Started/c. Installation Guide.md`. Do NOT use the in-container `/app/guide/...` path in markdown cross-references — those are for runtime mounts, not human-readable paths.

### Distinction from development docs

- **`development/`** — roadmaps, phase files, sprints, epics. Audience: engineers planning and tracking implementation work. Format: checklists, roadmap docs, per-phase implementation detail.
- **`guide/`** — operator manuals. Audience: anyone operating an MDC or onboarding to the platform. Format: prose walkthroughs, step-by-step guides, reference material.

A doc that tells you "here's what we're going to build and when" belongs in `development/`. A doc that tells you "here's how to use what already exists" belongs in `guide/`.

### Runtime rendering (skyy-command admin UI)

The skyy-command Django backend mounts `mdc-master-planning/guide/` into the Django pod via hostPath and exposes it to the admin UI SPA via the `/api/docs/structure` and `/api/docs/content/...` endpoints. The SPA never touches the filesystem directly — it consumes JSON from the API. Moving or renaming guide content is safe for the SPA as long as the Django hostPath mount keeps pointing at the right directory.

Implementation details:
- **Host path** (outside the pod): `/opt/skyy-net/mdc-master-planning/guide`
- **Pod path** (inside the container): `/app/guide` (read-only)
- **Chart**: `deployments/common/django/chart/templates/deployment.yaml` defines the `guide` volume + volumeMount
- **Values**: `deployments/common/django/chart/values.yaml` has `volumes.guidePath` which is substituted by Genesis from the `MASTER_PLANNING_GUIDE_PATH` placeholder in `lib/temporal/modules/common/provision/genesis_helper.py:_build_container_template_placeholders`
- **Python constant**: `backend/utils/path_manager.py:GUIDE_ROOT` resolves to `/app/guide` when it exists, else falls back to the host layout so local dev still works
- **Django view**: `backend/app/api/views.py:DOCS_ROOT` is an alias for `GUIDE_ROOT` (local name kept for readability within the view module)

### History

Prior to 2026-04-15, the guide lived at `skyy-command/docs/official_documentation/` — inside the skyy-command repo, mixed with developer-oriented architectural notes. It was moved to `mdc-master-planning/guide/` to consolidate all human-readable documentation in one place and to match the other cross-repo documentation conventions.

## Documentation Lifecycle

1. **Create all roadmaps up front** — every domain should have a roadmap.md before detailed planning begins, so the master roadmap can be built from real scope, not hypotheticals
2. **Create phase files when starting work** — don't fully detail all phase files up front; create each one when you begin that phase (roadmaps provide the high-level plan until then)
3. **Edit as you go** — phase files are living documents; update them as decisions are made and steps complete
4. **Mark complete honestly** — a checkbox means "done and verified," not "I think this works"
5. **Fill gaps when discovered** — if you find a missing doc while working, create it before proceeding
6. **Dispose of follow-ups immediately** — discovered something that needs follow-up? Fix it in place, or surface it in your report for PR-review triage per [Deferred Work](#deferred-work--github-issues-binding). Never leave it as a mental note.
7. **Update the Installation Guide whenever a completed phase changes operator-facing steps.** The guide at `guide/02. Getting started!/c. Installation Guide.md` is the executable version of the [MDC Rollout Standard](../architecture/mdc_rollout_standard.md). If an operator can't follow the guide linearly through Rollout Phases 0–4, the phase ordering is wrong — pause and reconcile before continuing. When closing a sprint sub-item, confirm whether its completion changed anything operator-facing; if so, the guide update is part of closing the sub-item, not a follow-on task.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Quality Checks

Before considering a phase file complete:

- [ ] All checkboxes are marked and verified
- [ ] Testing steps have been executed (not just written)
- [ ] Dependencies on other phases are satisfied
- [ ] No hardcoded paths or environment-specific values (per architecture standard)
- [ ] The phase achieves a logical stopping point of functionality
- [ ] Every follow-up discovered during the work is disposed — fixed in place, or surfaced in the report for PR-review triage (not left inline in the phase doc)
- [ ] Installation Guide updated for any operator-facing change introduced by the phase (or a note on the phase doc stating "no operator-facing change")

**Editing discipline — any doc, any edit (binding):** when an edit **moves, renames, or rescopes a term** (a credential's store, a count, a section reference, a renamed concept), grep the whole doc for the **OLD** term and confirm zero survivors before closing. A binding-section update that leaves prose or example stragglers ships a self-contradiction. And when an edit **reverses a binding standard section**, grep the **`development/` tree** for docs citing that section, not just the one doc — a reversal's stragglers live in the *other* docs that cited the old rule (the Vault §1 reversal left "Transit is binding" in `phase2_secrets_migration.md` + a `transit` exemplar in Logging §4.8 that took several conformance passes to surface).

## Cross-References

### Link form for `§N` references (binding)

When a `§N` reference points to **another** standard or document, it MUST be a full markdown link of the form:

```
[Standard Name §N](relative/path/to/standard.md)
```

When `§N` is a **self-reference** (within the same document), the bare form `§N` is acceptable — the reader is already in the right doc and the link would be a self-loop.

**Rationale:** cross-document references benefit from one-click navigation; readers shouldn't have to grep across the corpus to find a sibling standard's section. Self-references don't need a link.

**Pragmatic carve-out — continuation references:** when a paragraph or list item already contains a markdown link to the target document, subsequent bare `§N` continuations within the same paragraph or list item are acceptable. The click-through navigation is already provided by the established link, and forcing every `§N` to be a separate link duplicates the URL and clutters the prose. The continuation `§N` MUST refer to the same target document already linked in that paragraph or list item; it MAY refer to a different section of that document (e.g., the established link is to `§6.3` but the continuation reads "...and §6.4 covers retry semantics"). A continuation `§N` that refers to a *different* document (one not linked in the current paragraph or list item) is NOT covered by the carve-out — apply the strict rule and add a markdown link. Example acceptable forms:

- `[Architecture Standard](./architectural_standard.md) — §2 binds desired-state intent, §4 names the three execution paths, §10 forbids hardcoded paths.`
- `Per the [Tailscale Standard](../tailscale/tailscale_standard.md), §3 ACL-as-code and §9 one-tailnet-per-MDC are both binding.`

The pragmatic carve-out applies WITHIN a paragraph or list item; once a new paragraph or list item begins, the bare `§N` re-becomes a candidate for the strict rule.

**Anchor handling:** prefer the file-root form `[Standard §N](path.md)` over the fragment form `[Standard §N](path.md#section-anchor)` for now — adding section-anchor slugs corpus-wide is a separate audit not yet completed. File-root + §-prose is the canonical form.

**Forbidden:**
- ❌ A bare `§N` cross-document reference where the target standard isn't linked anywhere in the same paragraph or list item — readers cannot navigate from the reference. Example: `Per Architecture Standard §2.1 the canonical identifiers are k3s-N` (this should become `Per [Architecture Standard §2.1](./architectural_standard.md) the canonical identifiers are k3s-N`).
- ❌ A `§N` reference to a non-existent section in the target standard. If the target standard doesn't have `§N`, the link is broken information — fix the section number, fix the citation, or fix the source standard's structure.

### Footer section shape (binding)

Standards documents that link to peer standards use a footer section at the end of the document. Canonical shape:

```
## References

- [Standard Name](relative/path/to/standard.md) — one-line note describing the relationship or why this is referenced
- [Other Standard](relative/path) — one-line note
```

- **Heading:** `## References` is the canonical form. `## Related Documents` is an acceptable equivalent for documents that lean into a "see also" framing rather than citation. Other variants (`## Related`, `## See Also`, `## Related Standards`) should converge to `## References` opportunistically.
- **Bullets:** `- [Display Name](path) — one-line note`. Display name is the human-readable standard name (`Architecture Standard`, not `architectural_standard.md`) for cross-directory links; bare filename is acceptable when linking a sibling document in the same directory (e.g., `[networking_standard.md](./networking_standard.md)` from inside `standards/development/networking/`).
- **One-line note** justifies the link: what the target covers, what relationship it has to this standard, why a reader would follow it. "See for details" is too thin; "sibling: physical / L2 networking" is right.
- **Continuation references inside footer bullets** follow the §Cross-References pragmatic carve-out: the bullet's `[Standard Name](path)` link is the established link; subsequent bare `§N` continuations referring to that same target are acceptable within the bullet.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## CLAUDE.md Governance

`CLAUDE.md` files orient Claude sessions to a directory's purpose, conventions, and applicable standards. They are the entry point for any session working in that directory. Without a governance rule, the per-repo / per-component CLAUDE.md files drift away from the canonical standards index in `mdc-master-planning/CLAUDE.md`, and the question "which CLAUDE.md needs updating when a new standard lands?" gets answered by guesswork.

### Canonical CLAUDE.md tree

The platform has four roles for CLAUDE.md files. Each role has a different scope and a different rule for what it carries.

| File | Role | Owns | Does NOT own |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/opt/skyy-net/CLAUDE.md` | Workspace orientation | Multi-repo navigation, repo inventory, universal architecture pointer (e.g. "Architecture Standard governs all design") | Per-standard "read when" guidance — points at `mdc-master-planning/CLAUDE.md` for the full index |
| `mdc-master-planning/CLAUDE.md` | **Canonical standards index** | Every standard with "read when" guidance and "what breaking it looks like" | Per-repo filtering (every other CLAUDE.md handles that for itself) |
| Implementation repo CLAUDE.md (`skyy-command/`, `skyy-gate/`, `deploy-a-saurus/`, `mdc-ansible-collections/`, future service repos that publish code/images per [Repository Layout Standard §2](../architecture/repo_layout.md)) | Repo-scoped | Repo purpose + file layout + standards bound to code in THIS repo (filtered subset, by inclusion rule below) + repo-specific conventions | Standards content itself — always reference `mdc-master-planning`, never copy |
| Sub-component CLAUDE.md (e.g., `skyy-command/lib/temporal/CLAUDE.md`) | Sub-component-scoped | Sub-component scope + standards bound to code in THIS sub-component + sub-component-specific conventions | Broader-repo concerns; standards content itself |

Tooling-only CLAUDE.md files (`claude-dot-files/`) are out of scope for this governance — they govern Claude Code itself, not the platform.

### Inclusion rule (binding)

> **A repo or sub-component's CLAUDE.md MUST reference a standard if the standard's "Binding scope" includes any code path under that repo or sub-component. It MUST NOT reference a standard whose binding scope does not include any of its code paths.**

This is mechanical. Every standard already declares its binding scope at the top. The inclusion test reduces to "does the standard's binding scope mention paths under this CLAUDE.md's directory?"

Examples:
- `migration_standard.md` binding scope: "skyy-command/backend/ today; skyy-gate/gateway/django/ if it ever has its own DB; future Django installations." Inclusion: `skyy-command/CLAUDE.md` MUST reference it. `skyy-gate/CLAUDE.md` does not yet (no Django backend yet) but MUST when SkyyGate adds one. `deploy-a-saurus/CLAUDE.md`, `mdc-ansible-collections/CLAUDE.md`, etc. MUST NOT reference it.
- `architectural_standard.md` binding scope: platform-wide. Inclusion: every implementation-repo CLAUDE.md references it.
- `das_standard.md` binding scope: "any DAS workflow code" — covers `deploy-a-saurus/` AND `skyy-command/lib/temporal/modules/deploy_a_saurus/`. Inclusion: BOTH `deploy-a-saurus/CLAUDE.md` AND `skyy-command/CLAUDE.md` (or its temporal sub-component CLAUDE.md) reference it.
- `tailscale_standard.md` binding scope: covers `skyy-command/lib/temporal/activities/tailscale/`. Inclusion: `skyy-command/CLAUDE.md`. Not `deploy-a-saurus/`, etc.

If a standard's binding scope is ambiguous about whether it includes a given repo's code, the standard's binding-scope line is the bug — fix the standard, then apply the rule.

### Every standard MUST declare a Binding scope (binding)

The inclusion rule above is mechanical **only because it has an input**. A standard with no `**Binding scope:**` line cannot be tested against any CLAUDE.md, so the rule silently degrades to guesswork for exactly that standard — and the reader cannot tell the difference between "no CLAUDE.md references this" and "nobody could work out which should."

**Every standard under `standards/` MUST carry a `**Binding scope:**` line near the top, after the Status line, naming the code paths it governs.** Authoring a new standard without one is incomplete, not merely untidy. Where a standard genuinely governs no code path — a corpus-level or process standard — it says so explicitly rather than omitting the line.

### The second-order prose check (binding)

**When adding or updating a CLAUDE.md entry for standard X, also read the surrounding prose in that CLAUDE.md and confirm it asserts nothing X contradicts.**

The inclusion rule governs *which standards are referenced*. It says nothing about whether the file's own prose — paths, directory conventions, component descriptions written before that standard existed — still agrees with them. A correct reference sitting above a stale convention claim reads as *more* authoritative than either, because the reference appears to vouch for the prose.

The recurring shape is a path convention that moved: a CLAUDE.md written before a layout decision keeps describing the old location, and the entry added later points at the standard that changed it. Fix the prose in the same edit; if it cannot be fixed there, the contradiction goes to whoever owns the standard, never left standing.

### Standards Governance (binding — the canonical in-corpus home; all "Standards Governance" links resolve HERE)

*(Homed here 2026-07-27 — corpus links previously pointed at three different targets, none of which defined the rule.)*

- **Standards documents (`standards/`) are a curated product with human-in-the-loop control.** Autonomous workflows and agents may SURFACE standards implications (gaps, drift, deviations, amendment candidates) but MUST NOT auto-create, auto-modify, or auto-stub standards artifacts. All standards changes land through the interactive session (PM3 + operator) for human review.
- **Architectural decisions are captured as standards docs, not numbered ADRs.** The methodology (trade-offs, rationale, alternatives, consequences) applies; the artifact is `standards/<topic>.md`. `standards/architecture/` holds system-architecture descriptions, never per-decision ADR files.
- **Planning artifacts (phase docs, roadmaps, loose-ends, epic breakdowns) are NOT covered by this rule** — they are dispatch-scope; engineers MAY edit them autonomously. When a phase doc contradicts a standard, the engineer updates the phase doc (the standard is binding) AND surfaces the standards-side amendment as a candidate for human review.
- **`sprints.md` is the exception to the planning carve-out** — see §Sprint plans below: operator-owned, PM3+human edits only; autonomous runs surface candidates, never write it.
- **Deferred/rejected standards findings are logged** in the CPI decisions log (claude-dot-files `docs/development/cpi-decisions.md` while that repo lives; its successor surface after the SkyyNet conversion) so decisions aren't re-litigated.

### Standard-authoring checklist (binding)

When authoring or amending a standard, the authoring PR (or the human-reviewed amendment per the §Standards Governance section above) MUST:

1. **Write the Binding scope clearly.** Name the code paths (or "platform-wide") that the standard governs. Vague scopes like "Django code" are not enough — name the repos and the path globs.
2. **Identify consuming repos and sub-components.** Apply the inclusion rule to determine which CLAUDE.md files need updating.
3. **Update each consumer's CLAUDE.md** to reference the standard, with a one-line "read when" trigger and what breaking it looks like (matching the shape used in `mdc-master-planning/CLAUDE.md`).
4. **Update `mdc-master-planning/CLAUDE.md`** — the canonical index always carries every active standard regardless of consumer.

The canonical index in `mdc-master-planning/CLAUDE.md` is the authoritative entry. Per-repo CLAUDE.md entries are filtered views of the canonical entry — same shape (read-when + breaking-it-looks-like), filtered by inclusion rule.

### Forbidden patterns

- ❌ **Duplicating standards content into a CLAUDE.md.** CLAUDE.md files reference standards; they do NOT copy them. A CLAUDE.md entry is "read this standard when X" — never the standard's binding rules themselves.
- ❌ **Referencing a standard whose binding scope does not include the repo's code.** A skyy-gate session shouldn't be told to read the DAS Standard if SkyyGate has no DAS code path. Spurious references add noise and make sessions less efficient.
- ❌ **Authoring a new standard without updating consuming CLAUDE.md files in the same PR.** This is the drift mechanism that makes the inclusion rule necessary in the first place.
- ❌ **Per-repo CLAUDE.md files re-deriving the canonical index.** If a repo's CLAUDE.md tries to be a comprehensive standards reference, it duplicates `mdc-master-planning/CLAUDE.md` and immediately starts drifting. Repo CLAUDE.md is filtered, not comprehensive.

### Audit and drift detection

A periodic audit pass (run when standards-folder shape stabilizes — e.g., end of a sprint that authored multiple new standards) walks every CLAUDE.md and verifies:

1. Every standard reference passes the inclusion rule (no spurious refs).
2. Every standard whose binding scope covers this CLAUDE.md's directory is referenced (no missing refs).
3. Every entry uses the canonical "read when X / what breaking looks like" shape.

The audit is currently manual. If drift becomes frequent, a small script (`bin/audit-claude-md.sh`) that parses standards' binding-scope lines and cross-checks per-repo CLAUDE.md references becomes a candidate Sprint 2-7+ tooling item.

## Repo structure documentation (binding)

Every implementation repository carries one canonical layout file:

- **Path:** `<repo-root>/docs/file_structure.txt`
- **Format:** ASCII tree with `#` inline comments explaining each path's purpose. Plain text, not markdown.
- **Scope:** entire repo. One file per repo; no sub-component or sub-directory layout files.
- **Maintenance:** kept current as files are added, moved, or removed. New entries MUST include an explanatory comment; existing comments MUST be preserved on edits.
- **CLAUDE.md pointer:** every implementation repo's CLAUDE.md MUST include a `## Repo structure` section pointing at the file with explicit read-it-first framing.

**Forbidden:**
- Layout files outside the canonical `docs/` location (e.g., at repo root, in `lib/<component>/`, or in any other sub-directory) — fragments the canonical view.
- Markdown extension (`.md`) — these are plain ASCII trees, not prose docs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Anti-patterns

- **Don't write narrative history** — docs are not journals, but completed checkboxes naturally show what was done and in what order. That's valuable context. What to avoid is prose like "on March 15th we decided to..." — let the checkboxes tell the story
- **Don't duplicate** — reference other docs instead of copying content
- **Don't pre-plan too far ahead** — later phases will change; keep them as brief roadmap entries until you start them
- **Don't mix concerns** — one doc per domain per phase; if a doc covers two domains, split it
- **Don't leave stale checkboxes** — if requirements changed, update the checkboxes to match reality
- **Don't scatter deferred work** — never park it in a phase doc, roadmap doc, or inline sprint comment. Deferred work is a file in `tracked/issues/` carrying a `repo:` field for where the work lands; everything else is fixed in place.
- **Don't let open issues accumulate** — an issue that survives a standup without a disposition is the failure mode the convention exists to prevent. Growth in the open-issue count is a signal to plan the work or to fix the tool that is filing it.
- **Don't create informal-triage holding buckets** — every observation surfaced during sprint work gets ONE of three dispositions on the spot: (a) addressed inline as part of the current work, (b) surfaced in the work artifact for PR-review triage, OR (c) explicitly rejected as not-a-real-finding (deleted, or noted-and-dismissed in the work artifact). "Add to a backlog for later evaluation" is NOT a fourth option — it is silent deferral, and produces graveyards (see the 270-line "Parallel Backlog" sub-section that accumulated in `sprint_1_loose_ends.md` Section 1-1 between 2026-04-15 and 2026-04-28 as the canonical anti-example). If the observation is large enough that quick triage isn't possible, file it as a tracked issue with a body that begins "Needs triage:" — that's still a stable-ID tracked item, not a holding-bucket entry.
